blocks.body:
What's NeverDestruct?

NeverDestruct is an extensive addon that brings a modifier-style and non destructive workflow to Blender as well as additionnal tools to overhaul the modelling experience. With its flagship Edit Poly modifier, every edits you make inside an Edit Poly layer is recorded, UVs, shapekeys, vertex groups, vertex colors and every topology changes, you do not need to use specific tools, everything is recorded, the addon constantly watches what happens to the object.

Instead of commiting to your changes, you can now iterate directly on the object itself inside the modifier by using the journal system, which is a node based representation of your edits. You can create branches, edit past operations, mute or reroute.

On top of that, NeverDestruct brings more modifiers and tools, such as the Edit Mesh modifier which is a simplified and more straightforward version of Edit Poly, meant for higher density meshes, Shape Keys/Weight Map modifiers which allow to edit the data of those at that point in the modifier stack, or Symmetry and FFD, which are improved versions of Mirror and Lattice. You will also find a dedicated N panel with more tools, including smoothing groups, gizmo constraints and gizmo extrusion, more tools in the context menu and an overhauled modifier panel featuring shared modifiers, copy and paste ability, adding modifiers to several objects at once, and more. 

Requirements

Blender 5.2. Compatibility is not guaranteed on earlier versions. 

Installation/Update

To install or update, find top left the Edit menu, then select “Preferences…”

Then go in “Get Extensions” and find the down arrow top right, then select ”Install from Disk…“

Then locate and select the downloaded NeverDestruct Zip file, and press “Install from Disk”

Base mesh and modifiers

The base mesh is your object's original mesh, this is the usual entry point for editing meshes in blender, it's evluated before any modifier.

Modifiers are evaluted on top of it, and always in the top -> bottom order.

Modifier types:

-Edit Poly: Record individual operations/steps, make branches, edit past values. Also record data like UV, Shapekeys, Vertex groups, Vertex colors.

-Edit Mesh: Store thre result. Iterate through individual modifiers. Also record data like UV, Vertex groups, Vertex colors. Shape keys is not supported at the moment.

-FFD: Lattice wrapper with more controls, automatically fits the selection above it (Edit layers automatically create vertex groups of their selection), overhauled UI for easier back and forth editing.

-Symmetry: Mirror wrapper, automatically adds an empty, better UI controls as well, shortcuts button to automatically select the gizmo/visualize it, and go back and forth from the object -> symmetry gizmo.

-Shape Keys: Dedicated modifier to store Shape Keys.

-Weight Map: Dedicated modifier to store vertex groups.

Modifiers selection/insertion

You can add a modifier at any point in the stack, to do that, you can click on the modifier's icon on the left, this selects the modifier (useful for modifiers like arrays that display the gizmo only while selected). Then, adding a modifier will add it below the selection.

Copy/pasting, sharing modifiers, instancing

The new modifier panel allows to copy modifiers, paste them on any object or paste it as an instance. An instanced modifeir is a shared modifier, they're basically 1 modifier active on several objects at once, the values are always the same between the objects, you can make it unique again via the dropdown menu, this detaches the modifier basically.

Vertex groups from selection

when using Edit Poly or Edit Mesh modifiers, you automatically create vertex goups from the selections that happen in these layers, this is handy when you work with FFDs, or through different modifiers that you stack, you're also free to just duplicate the layer to make it permanent.

 

Edit tools

Edit tools are accessible through any mean of editing, they're not exclusive to Edit Poly/Edit Mesh. The main features are:

 

-Gizmo constraints and extrusions, for move, rotation and scaling.

-"Caddy" style operators, instead of selecting first then intantly applying, the tool will open a moveable window with the operator's settings, while you can select/deselect, and then you can choose to apply or not.

-This panel features either built-in operators or fully custom ones, for some tools, you can choose which implementation you use (blender vs custom).

-Smoothing groups panel, which is basically a "shading" group, instead of marking edges as sharp, you can select polygons and define their groups. You stil can use sharp edges and even combine them with groups.

-Better selection system, instantly select ledges, or full objects.

-Auto crease from materials delimitations, allowing you to automatically create hard edges from the junction between 2 materials

Quick start with Edit Poly

Adding a layer: Select a mesh, open the modifier panel and choose add modifier -> Edit Poly

Edit it: Each modifier has a dedicated "active" button, for that active modifier, simply press tab, edit mode through the object modes or "edit" in the modifier itself to edit in that modifier.

Model: Model like usual, select faces, inset them, extrude the result, and go back to object mode. Edit Poly will store the individual operations.

Change the input: Set the base mesh active, edit at that layer, and start moving vertices around, once you're back in object mode, the edit poly will replay operations on that altered topology.

Open the Journal: In Edit Poly, at the very bottom you will find a button to open the Journal. Find the extrude node, and play with the values.

The Edit Poly panel

Editing: 

Edit, this enters the layer directly from the modifier panel, similar to pressing tab or changing object mode.

Stores:

This enables/disables these data types, it doesn't erase them, it only disables/enables.

Slow builds:

While the addon is optimized as much as possible and uses an incremental system, it has fallback mechanisms that might require to scan the full object after a change, this can be problematic for dense meshes, therefore you have the option to disable slow builds. Slow builds disabled does not mean the replay system is disabled, it only means that the fallback method is not enabled, instead, you have to manually press "build now" to build in this case.

Slow builds is by default disabled on objects with more than 100 000 faces, this is a setting the addon's preferences. 

Operation Replay:

Auto: Automatically choose between replay or the snapshot (explained in another subsection)

Force Replay: Attempts to replay, even if it's using optimistic ways to get results (such as topology position). This might still get denied if the system is unable to properly replay.

Use Snapshot: Forces the use of the snapshot, this will never be denied for any reason, the snapshot is a recovery mechanism, a capture of the mesh in its last good state. When using the snapshot, the replay system is disabled, the journal has no effects.

Take Snapshot Now: Take a snapshot of the mesh in this state, useful after journal edits, since normally snapshots are taken when leaving edit mode.

Refresh Replay: Replay all nodes

Open Journal: Open the journal window, to display all stored operations.

Output: Select all output nodes connected. Those output nodes are defined in the Journal window.

What is stored by Edit Poly

The addon constantly watches the mesh and knows when something happened to it, the modifier doesn't require a specific set of tools to store the changes applied to the object.

On top of topology edits, the addon stores data as well, UVs, Shape Keys, Vertex groups, Vertex colors, all are stored as well. However, groups and keys are always created globally, meaning you don't create a group or a key inside the layer itself, you create it on the object in object mode, what happens in the group is you set the value of that data.

 

Note: Shape Keys introduce a slowdown to the replay system of Edit Poly, for now I don't recommend having many shape keys. However as you can see, you are able to change the topology with shapekeys, unlike default blender.

Controls of the Journal

The Journal is an horizontal node based visualization of the operations stored within an edit poly modifier, you can find it in each Edit Poly modifier at the bottom of the modifier card.

At the top you will find controls:

Base: This shows the mesh that enters the modifier, understand it as the "base mesh" the modifier evaluates against

Final: This is the final state the mesh is in the modifier, this is the state of the mesh at the very last output node

Fast Preview: When viewing the mesh's state on an operation, this isolates only the affected area, useful for dense meshes

Show Targets: Each node have targets which defines on what it's applied, enabling this allows to see what the node targets

Live Update: Enabling this makes the modifier instantly evaluate when dragging the timeline, or when changing values, which can cause repeated evaluations slowing down performance. 

Follow Timeline: Enabling this attaches the view to the timeline. When draggin, the view will move to where you're pointing.

+ Output: Add a new output node after the currently selected node.

Frame: Focus the currently selected node

Timeline behavior:

Left clicking: Select and instantly preview the nodes when you release.

Right clicking: Move the view without previewing.

Node behavior:

M: mute nodes

x/del: delete nodes

F2: Rename node

Shift + select: add nodes to selection

ctrl + select: remove nodes from selection

Muting an output node will mute all nodes that is connected before it

The Journal doesn't allow to directly add nodes, the purpose is to define the flow, branches, or refine past operations, the only node you can add from the Journal is a new Output node, once you've added a new output, you can either directly activate it through the Journal, or through the Output selection in the Edit Poly panel.

 

Editing past operations

The nodes are by default collapsed and show only the values that aren't default, since they're not "hardcoded" to show only a set of values, nodes can show all possible values each operation accepts. To see all the controls, click "All settings" on the node, this will expand the node and reveal all controls.

Creating branches/using outputs

An output node is the exit point of a branch, the default one is "Final" (which you can rename to anything), while editing within Final, the output node addvances to the right and a new node takes its place.

When creating/using an output node, it can either be made as a "termination", or make it itself connected to other nodes. Connecting an output to other nodes allow you to quickly make edits before a certain point (for example, you might have made a mesh, and decided that modifying it before a certain point would be beneficial, you can open the Journal, make a new Output where you decide, connect the right side of it so that it's connected to the next node, and start editing in that branch, you're now editing in an earlier state, and those changes will get picked up by the Final node.

 

One other good use case of branches/different outputs is for support loops for example, you may want a base mesh allowing easier deformation changes, but a final branch that adds support loops:

 

How non destructive is this?

The addon uses complex custom systems to make edits work and has different fallback mechanisms to try to save edits that are complex, as well as safety mechanisms, if for whatever reason a replay doesn't pass, it will automatically restore the mesh to a last known good snapshot.

Modifying an unaffected area should be safe, for example changing the other side of a modified cube:

 

What if changes break the replay?

If the replay cannot succeed, the modifier turns red, it automatically displays a snapshot version of the mesh

Opening the journal will reveal the nodes that can't succeed, the interesting thing about this system is that it allows you to repair or select any point before as a new output:

The warnings

Due to possibility range, the modifier has several warnings that indicate different things:

No warnings:

Attribute loss/Optimistic replay:

An attribute loss doesn't prevent the replay engine from correctly replaying mesh operations.

An optimistic replay happens when there is no direct proof anymore for the operations' targets, the results should be correct, and the replay is still in use, however this is a state where some changes such as moving topology might break some operations (due to no direct proof being accessible, one last way is to use the topology itself as a reference point, moving it therefore breaks this).

It is possible to accept the results, accepting the results means the warning will fade and the replay will work again like expected.

 

Anchored operation:

An anchored operation is an operation that did not succesfully map to an operator, for example, in normal operations, an extrude is stored and seen as an exturde, but an anchored operation means the addon saw a mesh edit, but could not pinpoint what caused it, this is not expected and not normal, an anchored replay is basically a direct "change", meaning it won't correctly adapt to upstream changes.

 

Replay failure, snapshot is used:

Replay failure, the modifier is using a stored snapshot, no replay is performed, upstream deformations won't propagate, the snapshot is a "fixed" mesh state, this is a recovery situation, instead of corrupting the mesh or breaking it, it allows you to make sure your mesh is safe.

However you can at any time solve a replay failure, fixing the upstream topology to be back to what that modifier was expecting will make it work again, or, fixing the nodes in the journals/muting the new nodes that make that output fail, will alos make ti work again.

The snapshot system

Everytime the system has recorded an operation and validated it, it stores a snapshot of the mesh, this is needed to make sure the mesh cannot be broken by upstream changes, or journal changes. However, journal edits do not automatically update the snapshot, meaning if you change for example an extursion, or a bevel, and break the mesh, it will get restored to the last state that branch was when exiting edit mode (where the validation happens). For this reason, there is a dedicated "take snapshot now" button which ensures that the mesh is saved in this state. Snapshots are by default stored per output node, meaning each possible outcomes is saved.

Using other addons' tools

Normally it should register all tools, however it's possible an addon's tool is not directly seen/recorded, when this happens, the addon automatically prompts you and ask if you would like to accept this new tool in the replay system. If you don't, the edits will be stored as anchored nodes. The allowed tools can be found in the addon's preferences (Edit -> Preferences -> Add-ons -> NeverDestruct -> "Recorder Policy Overrides"

Limitations/Performance

The only drawback of the current Edit Poly is the performance impact on dense topology, right now I recommend working with Edit Poly on low/medium density meshes, think below 50k faces (at the entry of the modifier, subdivisions or anything after doesn't impact), higher density remains usable/workable, but it's not at the performance target I'm currently aiming.

Another limitation is that right now, slow scenes negatively impact the replay speed, so I also recommend working in scenes that aren't lagging.

Performance is a big priority for me, and I have ideas/plans for this, however this requires time and investigation, which is why those ideas aren't implemented yet.

Edit Mesh

Edit mesh is there to fill in the gap with Edit Poly's current limitations, it's a lightweight version that has not as non destructive, but still stores all the usual changes. The speed boost lies in the fact it doesn't replay operations, it only stores the result of your edits, it still uses a custom system however to allow for more non destructiveness, it is for example, possible to iterate on differences areas of the same meshes in 2 layers:

Edit Mesh can store attributes like Vertex groups and Vertex colors, however right now it doesn't store Shape keys, you can however use the Shape keys modifier for that

Shape Keys 

The Shape Keys modifier can store in Relative or Absolute mode, in Relative, the changes you make can stack up, one modifier might define a translation for a group, and another one can build on top of that, disabling the 1st one would therefore visibly affect the 2nd one's result as well.

Create a shape key in object mode, and add a Shape Keys modifier, select the Shape Key and enter edit mode.

Weight Map

A Weight Map modifier can store in 2 different ways, Relative or Absolute, relative means whatever data is added to what it receives, meaning you can combine Weight Map modifiers for example

FFD

An FFD is basically an improved lattice modifier, it automatically adds a lattice in the scene, wraps it around a vertex group (it defaults to the edit poly's vertex group just above where it's inserted).

You get 2 new quick controls for this modifier, the left one is to view the lattice, the one on the right to edit it. The modifier panel is also overhauled for this modifier, allowing a more intuitive interface to instantly edit the lattice and go back to the main mesh.

An FFD is not locked to one object, it can be shared across several ones, it automatically wraps around the selection.

 

Symmetry

Symmetry is also basically a wrapper, but for the mirror modifier this time. It automatically adds an empty attached to the object, implements a custom gizmo viewer to visualize the symmetry axis, and also features a custom and more intuitive way to go from the main object to the empty/symmetyr gizmo
